title: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man? sun → moon → fire → speech → self (4.3)
hook: a king asks what light a person has, and takes the lights away one at a time
tomorrow: dreaming — the self creates its own world

segments.voice: Yesterday: murdha, the head. Shakalya pushed past the limit as someone else's tool. Your line was don't ask past the limit.

The power goes out at night. The streetlights die, the screens go black, your phone is at one percent and then it's gone. You can't see your own hand. Then, from the next room, someone calls your name, and you get up and walk toward the voice. Something very like that moment is in the Brihadaranyaka, in a talk between a king and a sage with no crowd and no cows: King Janaka, asking one question and taking the lights away one by one.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T SEE YOUR HAND.` → `YOU WALK TOWARD THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: The debate is over. In book four, Yajnavalkya visits the king again, quietly. Yajnavalkya, Janaka asks, what light does a person have? The sun, your majesty. By the light of the sun a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. True. But when the sun has set, what light does a person have? The moon. And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire has gone out? Speech. That's why, when you can't even see your own hand, wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. True, Yajnavalkya. And when the sun and the moon have set, the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does a person have then? And Yajnavalkya says: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati. The self is their light. By the light of the self a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. Which is the self? The one made of knowing, among the senses, the light within the heart. Each light is real, and each one can go out. The question is what's left when all of them are gone. Sit in a dark room with your eyes open: nothing to look at, and still something knows it's dark. In the text's terms, that knowing is the self, the light under all the others.
screen: `THE SUN, THE MOON, THE FIRE.` · `SPEECH: WE WALK TOWARD A VOICE.` · `THE SELF IS THEIR LIGHT.` · `THE LIGHT WITHIN THE HEART.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and take the lights away in the king's order: let the sun set, then the moon, then let a small fire go out. Listen for a voice, near or far, the light you'd walk toward in the dark; then let even the voices go quiet, outside and inside, and rest in whatever is left without naming it.
Jyotis, light. The king's question and the sage's answer: when every outer light is gone, jyotis, the light a person still has, is the self.
Your line: your own light. Next, the light that shows a dream. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu homes and temples light lamps at dawn and dusk and at festivals, and teachers sometimes quote the Brihadaranyaka's line that the self is a person's own light when explaining the inner meaning of the lamp.

match.prompt: the lights, in order — tap the pairs.

myth: in Janaka's list, the last outer light is fire
after fire comes speech: in the dark, you go toward a voice.
Yajnavalkya calls the self the light within the heart
the one made of knowing, among the senses.
when every outer light is gone, the text says a person has no light

fork.setup: it's pitch dark. no sun, no moon, no fire. you can't see your own hand. how does the text say you find your way?
fork.reveal: wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. speech is a light too, until it falls silent and only the self is left.

original.note: Sanskrit jyotis: light. ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati, the self is their light (4.3.6).

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle about the sun and the moon.
what it means: every outer light can go out; what is left, and was there all along, is the self.
what a scholar hears: kiṃjyotir ayaṃ puruṣa (4.3.2): the light-sequence leads to the self as 'the light within the heart' (hṛdy antarjyotiḥ, 4.3.7).

a sacred flame kept burning at home

chat.says: If the sun, the moon and every fire went out, what light would be left?
options: The text says the self is our light, the knowing within the heart.
Speech is the last light; we always walk toward a voice in the dark.
None at all; once speech is gone, a person is left in darkness.
chat.meaning: After the sun, moon, fire and speech, Yajnavalkya answers: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati, the self is their light.

Janaka.meaning: the king who asks Yajnavalkya what light a person has

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage who answers the challengers in Janaka's court

Brihadaranyaka.meaning: one of the oldest and longest Upanishads

notes: 4.3.1 says Yajnavalkya came to Janaka intending not to speak, but Janaka had earlier been granted a boon to ask anything; this framing is omitted. Confirm whether it should be included.
The sequence of lights (4.3.2–6) is paraphrased; the speech line ('when one cannot see one's own hand, where a voice is raised, there one goes') follows 4.3.5 closely. Confirm.
Sanskrit transliterated without diacritics: ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati.

Reviewer edit: the hook no longer says the dark-room moment is in the text 'nearly word for word' (only the walking-toward-a-voice line, 4.3.5, is close). The teach no longer says book four 'opens' with this scene: 4.1–4.2 (Yajnavalkya and Janaka on six partial definitions of Brahman, and the self as neti neti) come first; 4.3 is a later visit.
